blocks.text: *Görogly* is the great heroic epic of the Turkmens: a cycle of stories in prose and verse about the hero Görogly, his forty young horsemen, his wife and his horse. It has no single author. It belongs to generations of singers, and the same hero, under names such as Köroğlu and Gurughli, appears in the tales of many peoples, from the Caucasus and Anatolia to Central Asia.

**The story.** In Turkmen the hero's name is usually translated as **son of the grave**. Görogly gathers forty brave young men, the *ýigitler*, and builds a stronghold, Çandybil, from which they ride out on their adventures. His winged horse, Gyrat, is almost a hero in its own right. In one of the best-known episodes he sees a fairy, Agaýunus, in a dream and sets out to find her; she becomes his wife. Through all the adventures the epic praises bravery, honesty, friendship and fairness, and the hope for freedom and justice.

**The singers.** The epic lives in performance. Its singers, the *bagşy*, perform it seated, playing the *dutar*, the two-stringed lute, or the *gyjak*, a bowed fiddle. They tell the story in prose and sing its poems, and each adds touches of his or her own; women perform it as well as men. A master teaches pupils, who learn by listening and by performing in public. Within Turkmenistan the tradition is strongest in the north and east, in Daşoguz and Lebap provinces.

**An oral encyclopaedia.** UNESCO describes the epic as a kind of oral encyclopaedia: besides adventure, it carries old knowledge of customs, of raising livestock and of traditional healing. In 2015 the epic art of Görogly was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Its performers take part in festivals and in yearly competitions between Görogly singers.

blocks.title: Legend, not history
blocks.text: Görogly is a hero of legend. Some historians link the wider Köroğlu legend to a man who may have lived in the 16th century, and most versions were written down from singers from the 18th century on; but each singer's Görogly differs, and the tales are best read as tales.
With this unit's grammar, you can read this:

blocks.tk: Görogly batyr ýigit eken. Ol kyrk ýigidi bilen Çandybilde ýaşapdyr. Gyrata münüp, uzak ýurtlara gidipdir. Bagşy dutar çalyp, Görogly hakda aýdym aýdýar. Men çagakam bu dessany atamdan eşitdim.
blocks.en: Görogly was a brave young man, they say. He lived in Çandybil with his forty young men. He would mount Gyrat and ride off to distant lands. The bagşy plays the dutar and sings about Görogly. When I was a child, I heard this epic from my grandfather.
